title: ALPN callback function sometimes leads to segfault in node.js >= 18.13.0
body: I am running Node.js 18.15.0 on 64-bit Ubuntu Linux. My TLS server rarely segfaults in production, around one request per million, and I have not found a local reproducer. The stack traces consistently pass through SSL_select_next_proto, SelectALPNCallback, and tls_handle_alpn. I captured another crash and extracted a Kubernetes core dump, but the release binary does not have the debug symbols I need for full local values. I can add instrumentation or collect more information if I know what to inspect. The server should reject bad input rather than segfault.

symptoms_visible: My Node.js 18.15.0 TLS server occasionally exits with SIGSEGV in production, usually after a stack through SSL_select_next_proto, SelectALPNCallback, and tls_handle_alpn.
I see roughly one crash per million requests and have not reproduced it locally.
N0.label: N0 rare production ALPN segfault reported

symptoms_visible: The production process still occasionally segfaults at SSL_select_next_proto+76 while handling a TLS ClientHello.
N1.label: N1 crash registers and stack collected

symptoms_visible: The same production segfault continues even though the captured ClientHello contains a normal ALPN list with h2 and http/1.1.
Replaying the captured message locally for one million iterations does not crash.
N2.label: N2 valid ALPN and production-only behavior established

symptoms_visible: With ALPNProtocols set to an empty array, production processes can still segfault under representative traffic.
N2_x.label: N2_x empty ALPN workaround aftermath

symptoms_visible: After deploying Node.js 18.12.0 across ten production servers, I have seen zero core dumps, while newer versions crashed about hourly with the default ALPN configuration.
Other affected production deployments also remain stable on 18.12.x and crash after upgrading.
N3.label: N3 version boundary confirmed in production

symptoms_visible: With two overlapping TLS connections, both callbacks receive the same callback-argument value from the shared context.
An affected production environment running the candidate fix no longer crashes under the workload that previously triggered the failure.
N4.label: N4 shared callback argument and candidate fix verified

symptoms_visible: The TLS server remains stable under representative production traffic on a build containing the callback-lifetime fix; the SSL_select_next_proto segfault no longer occurs.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

question_patterns: Can you run disassemble and info registers on the top SSL_select_next_proto frame, and include a hex dump of the first 32 or 64 stack bytes?
Please share the faulting instruction, register values, and a short stack-memory dump from the core.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The crash is at SSL_select_next_proto+76: `movzbl (%rax),%eax`. In this core, rax/rdi/rdx are `0x75684f4f7156766e`, r14 is 12, and r15 is `0x7f499574c150`. I also dumped the SSL_select_next_proto and ALPN callback frames and their stack words.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The fault is inside my JavaScript callback after OpenSSL has returned normally; SSL_select_next_proto is not on the crashing stack.
The same instruction faults, but the invalid pointer value differs in another core.

question_patterns: Does the address in rax point to readable memory in the core?
Can GDB examine the memory being dereferenced by the faulting instruction?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: No. When I ask GDB to examine the address in rax, it says memory at that address is not available. Every core I checked fails on the same dereference instruction.

edges.comment: The reporter supplied raw disassembly, registers, frame data, and stack words requested by the maintainer. Interpretation of the invalid pointer's lifetime remains engineer-side.

question_patterns: Can you recover the TLS handshake bytes associated with a crash and share or decode the ClientHello?
Please capture the ClientHello that reaches a crashing connection, especially the raw ALPN extension.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I recovered the full 512-byte TLS record from the core and decoded it. The ALPN extension is `0010 000e 000c 02 6832 08 687474702f312e31`, which is h2 and http/1.1. I checked three dumps and all three have a valid ALPN record.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The crashing packet has a zero-length or truncated ALPN protocol list that ends outside the ClientHello.
The valid protocol list contains only http/1.1 rather than h2 and http/1.1.

question_patterns: Can you replay that captured ClientHello locally in a loop and report whether it crashes?
Does the exact handshake reproduce outside the production workload?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I replayed the full message locally in a single-threaded loop for one million iterations and nothing failed. It still happens in production, but I cannot trigger it in the local stress test.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The exact packet crashes a fresh local server every time on its first connection.

edges.comment: The packet bytes rule out the early empty or malformed ALPN hypothesis. The captured handshake and replay result are reporter-produced evidence, not a root-cause conclusion.

solution.intent: Avoid the crash by configuring the HTTPS server with an empty ALPNProtocols array.
solution.concrete_example: Set `ALPNProtocols: []` in the options passed to `https.createServer()`.

edges.comment: The original reporter initially saw fewer crashes with an empty ALPN list, but another affected production user later confirmed that the same crash still occurs with this setting. Multi-user evidence is folded into one simulated user side.

question_patterns: Can you compare production behavior with a Node.js version from before the ALPN callback change?
Please deploy the last known older version under the same workload and report the crash count.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reverted ten production servers to Node.js 18.12.0. They have produced zero core dumps since the deployment. With newer versions and default ALPN, I was seeing about one core dump per hour.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Node.js 18.12 crashes at the same rate under the same production traffic.
The older deployment is 18.12.1 rather than 18.12.0 and remains equally stable.

question_patterns: What code change or version boundary are you comparing against?
Which TLS-related change first appears in the versions that crash?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The behavior changes at the ALPN callback optimization introduced for the releases after 18.12. The screenshot is the change I suspected: before it, the callback recovered TLSWrap from the SSL object; afterward, a callback argument was passed through the context.

edges.comment: This was a persistent production rollback, so the system state changes. At this state, another affected production user also volunteered that setting ALPNProtocols to an empty array did not prevent the crash. Other affected users independently reported that 18.12.x was stable while later 18.x and 20.x builds crashed under production load.

question_patterns: Since the empty ALPN configuration is not reliable, can you compare the same workload on a version from before the behavior began?
Please roll a production group back to the older Node.js line and report whether the crashes continue.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reverted ten production servers to Node.js 18.12.0 and have seen zero core dumps since then. Other affected deployments also report that 18.12.x stays stable while versions after that crash.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The older Node.js version continues to crash at the same rate.

question_patterns: Which source change aligns with the first crashing versions?
What changed in the ALPN callback between the stable and unstable versions?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The first unstable versions contain the ALPN callback optimization. The older code obtained TLSWrap from the SSL object, while the newer code passes a callback argument through the SSL context.

edges.comment: Recovery path after the empty-ALPN workaround is falsified. The destination preserves the falsification fact while adding the production rollback evidence. The image was already used on the canonical version-comparison edge and is not duplicated here.

question_patterns: Can you pause two overlapping TLS connections and inspect the callback argument received for each one?
Please open connection A, then complete and close connection B before sending A's ClientHello, and compare the callback-argument values in GDB.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I opened connection A, waited, opened B, sent B's ClientHello, closed B, waited again, and then sent A's ClientHello. With a breakpoint on SelectALPNCallback, both connections had the same value in r9, the callback argument stored in SSL_CTX.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Each overlapping connection consistently receives a distinct callback argument that points to its own live TLSWrap.
The same shared callback-argument value appears with shorter delays between the two connections.

question_patterns: In a production core, does the callback argument still point to a valid TLSWrap object?
Can you inspect the SSL context's stored ALPN callback argument at the time of the crash?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: In the production core, the TLSWrap and SSL objects involved still look intact, but `ssl->ctx->ext.alpn_select_cb_arg` points to memory that no longer looks like a TLSWrap object.

question_patterns: Can you test the candidate patched build under the production workload that normally triggers this crash?
Please deploy the proposed fix to a representative production group and report whether the SSL_select_next_proto crashes continue.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tested the candidate fix with the affected production workload, and it resolves the crash. That workload normally crashes about once per two million HTTP requests.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The candidate build still crashes in SSL_select_next_proto at the same production rate.

edges.comment: The controlled connection sequence and core inspection came from another affected production user, and verification came from a further affected deployment; all are folded into one simulated user side. These are raw observations. Concluding that a connection-specific TLSWrap pointer was stored in shared SSL_CTX state is engineer inference.

solution.intent: Fix the ALPN callback lifetime bug by no longer treating a connection-specific TLSWrap pointer as the callback argument stored on the shared SSL_CTX; recover the wrapper from the current SSL connection instead, then have the affected deployment verify a build containing the fix.
solution.concrete_example: Apply the callback fix from the accepted patch so SelectALPNCallback obtains TLSWrap from the current SSL object rather than a per-connection pointer retained in the shared SSL_CTX callback argument. Test the resulting build under representative concurrent TLS traffic before declaring the incident resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the invalid dereference, valid ClientHello, version boundary, shared r9 value, and stale-looking callback argument. Engineers connected those facts: the optimized callback stored a particular TLSWrap pointer as an argument on an SSL_CTX shared by connections, so another connection could replace that pointer and then be collected before the first connection parsed its ClientHello. Recovering TLSWrap from the current SSL object's app data avoids the stale shared-context pointer.

edges.comment: Final accepted diagnosis and fix from the issue tail. Release scheduling and backport discussion are deliberately excluded from scoring.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause: the optimized ALPN callback stored a connection-specific TLSWrap pointer as callback data on an SSL_CTX shared by multiple TLS connections, allowing the pointer to become stale before another connection's ClientHello was parsed.

Must ground the diagnosis in the collected evidence: the invalid SSL_select_next_proto dereference, valid ALPN records, stability before the callback optimization, overlapping connections receiving the same context callback argument, and a crash core where that argument no longer resembles a TLSWrap.
Must fix the lifetime/ownership error by obtaining TLSWrap from the current SSL connection rather than relying on the connection-specific pointer stored in shared SSL_CTX callback state.
Must not treat a malformed or zero-length ALPN record as the final diagnosis, because captured crashing ClientHellos had valid h2/http/1.1 ALPN data.
Must not present ALPNProtocols: [] as the fix, because affected production traffic still crashed with that configuration.
Must have an affected user verify a build containing the callback-lifetime fix under representative production load before treating the issue as resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Production operator and application developer with limited C++ and assembly expertise, but capable of extracting Kubernetes core dumps, using GDB, decoding TLS records, compiling custom builds, and running controlled production comparisons. Evidence from several similarly affected operators is folded into the same user side.
persona_hint.communication_style: Persistent, candid, and highly cooperative; shares raw traces and experiments in detail, labels speculation as uncertainty, and relies on maintainers to interpret low-level lifetime and OpenSSL behavior.
